turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The tourbillon is probably the most famous complication in watchmaking. But what does it actually do?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It was invented by Abraham-Louis Breguet, and he patented it in eighteen oh one. Back then, people carried pocket watches, usually standing up in a vest pocket.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Because gravity pulls on the balance wheel and its spring. When a watch stays in one position for hours, gravity can make it run a little fast or slow. Watchmakers call this positional error.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It tries to. The balance and escapement are put inside a small rotating cage called a carriage. Usually it turns once a minute. So the errors in different positions cancel each other out, more or less.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But today we wear watches on our wrists, and our wrists move all the time.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's the big debate. Many experts say a wristwatch changes position so often that the tourbillon isn't really necessary. A well-made watch without one can be just as accurate.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So why are they so popular?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Because it's beautiful to watch. You see that tiny cage spinning through a window in the dial. It shows great skill. For most buyers today, the tourbillon is more art than function, and that's perfectly fine.
